Ear training · no sheet music needed

Hearing intervals

Sing the first two notes of “Somewhere Over the Rainbow.” Now the first two of “Twinkle, Twinkle.” Your voice just made two different jumps — one huge, one medium — and you did it without reading a note of music.

The size of a jump like that is called an interval, and each size has its own sound. Three sizes — thirds, fifths, and octaves — carry most of the melodies you know. This lesson trains you to call them by name.

§1

Three leaps, three songs

Each leap below gets the same treatment: hear it bare, then hear it start a song you know — the song is how you’ll remember the leap. Once you own one, you start calling pairs cold.

Anchor 1 · the biggest leap

The octave — the same note, higher

“Some-where” over the rainbow.

Play the bare pair a few times and hum both notes. The top note is the bottom note over again — higher, yet unmistakably the same note. That sameness is the whole test: when a leap lands on the same note, higher, it’s an octave. And the first leap of “Somewhere Over the Rainbow” — some-WHERE — is exactly this jump, which makes that song your permanent label for it.

Anchor 2 · the open leap

The perfect fifth — new note, hollow ring

“Twin-kle twin-kle” — the jump between the two words.

This pair lands on a genuinely new note — hum both, and the sameness test fails. Yet the two notes sound open and settled together, almost hollow. That leap is the perfect fifth, and you already know it cold: it’s the jump between the first “twinkle” and the second. (It also opens the Star Wars theme, if you know that one better.) And “perfect” is just part of the fifth’s traditional name — a label, not a grade.

Anchor 3 · the small leap

The major third — small, warm, bright

“Oh, when the saints” — “Oh” up to “when.”

The smallest leap of the three, and the sweetest. Where the fifth sounds open and neutral, the third sounds warm — it’s the note that makes a major chord sound happy. Sing “Oh, when the saints go marching in”: the small bright step from “Oh” up to “when” is a major third. (“Major” marks the exact size — there’s a slightly smaller, sadder third for another day.)

All three on one ladder

Each rung is a half-step: the smallest move between two neighboring piano keys. Every leap is a reach up the ladder.

Before you click anything: all three leaps below start from the same low note. Hum where you think each one lands, then play it and check yourself.

§2

When the song won’t tell you

So far, each leap arrived right after its lesson. Real songs don’t do that — a leap just happens, and you work it out cold. Two checks, always in this order:

1 · The sameness check. Hum the low note, then the high one. The same note, higher? Octave — done. This check is instant, and it clears the biggest leap out of the way first.

2 · The anchor sing. Not the same note? Sing “twin-kle twin-kle,” starting on the low note. If the song’s leap matches yours, it’s a fifth. If the song’s leap falls clearly short of your “twin-kle,” try “Oh, when” — landing there means a major third.

You don’t need a good voice for any of this. A shaky hum works fine — you’re comparing two notes, not performing.

One more thing, and it’s what makes the anchors so useful: always sing from the song’s own low note, wherever it sits. The anchors measure the distance between the two notes, not the notes themselves — so they work no matter which note a song starts on.

Quick Reference

Octave — 12 stepsThe top note is the bottom note over again, higher. Hum both and they blend into one name.Anchor: “Some-where” (Over the Rainbow). Men and women singing one melody together are an octave apart.
Perfect fifth — 7 stepsA genuinely new note, but open, settled, hollow with the first one.Anchor: “twin-kle twin-kle” (or the Star Wars opening). A power chord is a loud fifth.
Major third — 4 stepsSmall, warm, bright — the note that makes a major chord happy.Anchor: “Oh, when” the saints. Falls clearly short of a “twin-kle” sung from the same low note.
StepThe smallest gap between two neighboring piano keys — one rung of the ladder. Musicians call it a half-step or semitone.You never count steps by ear; the counts just explain why the leaps sound bigger and smaller.
The routine1 — Sameness check: hum both notes; the same note higher means octave, done. 2 — Anchor sing: from the low note, try “twin-kle” (fifth), then “Oh, when” (third).Always sing from the song’s own low note. Anchors measure distance, so they work from any starting note.
